subject: Biology
title: Germ Theory: A Revolution
description: A short lesson to help you apply Germ Theory: A Revolution.

hook.text: Before the 1860s, doctors didn't wash their hands between patients. Infections were a mystery.

buildup.text: Louis Pasteur showed that microbes cause fermentation and spoilage—not spontaneous generation.

discovery.text: Robert Koch proved specific bacteria cause specific diseases, establishing Koch's postulates.

twist.text: When Semmelweis urged hand-washing in hospitals, fellow doctors ridiculed and rejected him.

climax.text: Germ theory transformed medicine. Surgery, sanitation, and vaccines all followed from this idea.

punchline.text: Invisible germs were killing millions all along.

quiz.question: Who established that specific bacteria cause specific diseases?

details.summary: Germ theory, established by Pasteur and Koch in the 1800s, proved that microorganisms cause infectious disease. This replaced the miasma theory of disease from bad air and revolutionized medicine by introducing antiseptic surgery, vaccination, and public sanitation measures.
details.whyItMatters: Germ theory is arguably the most important breakthrough in medical history. It led to antiseptic surgery, pasteurization, vaccination, antibiotics, and public health infrastructure that together have saved billions of lives.
takeaways: Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation showing microbes come from microbes
Koch's postulates established the criteria for proving a microbe causes a disease
Germ theory led directly to antiseptic surgery, saving countless lives

faq.question: What did people believe caused disease before germ theory?
faq.answer: Miasma theory attributed disease to foul air from rotting matter. Other theories blamed imbalanced humors, punishment from gods, or astrological alignments. Without understanding microbes, handwashing, antiseptics, and water treatment seemed unnecessary.

faq.question: What are Koch's postulates?
faq.answer: Four criteria to prove a microbe causes a specific disease: the microbe must be found in all cases of the disease, isolated and grown in culture, cause the disease when introduced to a healthy host, and be re-isolated from the infected host.
